explanations.explanation: Yes, baker, it's his enemy. Jesus says, “…his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and slipped away.” (Matthew 13:25) Everybody's asleep, and somebody's out there doing the most unneighborly thing in history. No name tag, no note, just weeds.

Good guess, since fields usually have neighbors next to them. But Jesus never calls this person a neighbor. He says “his enemy” (Matthew 13:25), and later He explains the enemy is the devil (Matthew 13:39). So the farmer's problem is bigger than a fence dispute.

Hmm, I see why you'd think so, because workers are the ones who'd be in a field. But the servants don't show up until the weeds appear, and then they ask, “Where then did the weeds come from?” (Matthew 13:27) The owner answers, “An enemy did this…” (Matthew 13:28)

That's it, baker. The enemy sowed weeds among the wheat. The seed was the wheat's whole future, and he went and stuck weeds right in the middle of it. When the weeds appear, the servants ask, “Where then did the weeds come from?” (Matthew 13:27)

Barley sounds like a very farm-ish answer, I'll give you that. But the text doesn't say a word about barley. What the enemy sows among the wheat is weeds, and the servants ask, “Where then did the weeds come from?” (Matthew 13:27)

Flax is a fun guess, friend, but nobody in this parable plants it. I think I'd faint if a farmer found flax in his wheat and called it an enemy attack. No, this enemy comes while everyone is asleep, sows weeds among the wheat, and slips away (Matthew 13:25). Sneaking off like that is the move of someone who ate the last cookie and now whistles at the ceiling.

Close, but the order is the other way around. The weeds didn't beat the wheat out of the ground. Jesus says, “When the wheat sprouted and bore grain, then the weeds also appeared.” So the wheat was already growing before anybody noticed the weeds.

That's right, friend, it's false. Jesus says, “When the wheat sprouted and bore grain, then the weeds also appeared.” The wheat was already up and growing, and then the weeds showed up. It's the kind of surprise where everything looks fine, right up until it doesn't.

True, baker. The servants ask if they should pull the weeds, and the owner says, “No.” His instruction is, “Let both grow together until the harvest.” That's not what you'd expect a farmer to say, and it makes you want to hear why.

Ooh, so close, friend! The servants offer to go pull the weeds up, and the owner says, “No.” Then he gives his reason: “if you pull the weeds now, you might uproot the wheat with them.” (Matthew 13:29) So the weeds stay put for now. I once snatched a whole tray off the counter to save one crooked cookie and ended up with a pile of crumbs, so I felt that man's caution in my bones.

explanations.answer: They might uproot the wheat too
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The owner says, “if you pull the weeds now, you might uproot the wheat with them.” He's thinking about the good crop. Pull the wrong thing, and you lose what you were trying to protect.

explanations.answer: The weeds will die on their own
explanations.explanation: That's a hopeful guess, but the owner never says the weeds will die. What he says is to let both grow until the harvest, and then the weeds get collected and burned (Matthew 13:30). The reason he gives for waiting is the wheat.

explanations.answer: The servants need to rest first
explanations.explanation: Nice of you to look out for the servants, friend, but rest never comes up. The owner gives one reason, and it's about the wheat: “…you might uproot the wheat with them.” That's all the text says about why.

Close, but the owner has the order flipped from that. He tells the harvesters, “First collect the weeds and tie them in bundles to be burned; then gather the wheat into my barn.” The weeds get gathered first. The wheat goes into the barn after.

Yes, it's false, baker. The owner says, “First collect the weeds and tie them in bundles to be burned; then gather the wheat into my barn.” Weeds first, wheat second. The wheat ends up in the barn at the end.
Yes, burned. The owner says the weeds are collected and tied in bundles “…to be burned…” They're not wheat, and they don't go where the wheat goes. The wheat goes into his barn.
That would make for one very strange second season, friend. But the owner has no replanting in mind. He says the weeds are tied in bundles “…to be burned…”

explanations.answer: They will be sold at market
explanations.explanation: The owner isn't running a weed stand, baker. Once the harvesters collect the weeds and tie them in bundles, he says they are “…to be burned…” Selling is nowhere in his plan.

That's it, baker, a tree. Jesus says, “…it grows into the largest of garden plants and becomes a tree…” The smallest seed ends up as the largest garden plant. Not bad for something you could lose on your fingertip.
Vines are a fair guess for a garden plant. But Jesus says this seed “…becomes a tree…” It's the largest of the garden plants, and it's big enough for the birds of the air to nest in its branches.
Hmm, a reed would be a pretty modest finish for this seed, friend. Jesus says it “…becomes a tree…” The smallest of all seeds grows into the largest of garden plants.
True, friend. Jesus says it grows big enough that “…the birds of the air come and nest in its branches.” Think about that. The seed started so small, and now it's big enough to be a home for birds.
Not this time, baker. It's true. Jesus says the plant grows into a tree, “…so that the birds of the air come and nest in its branches.” That's how big the tiny seed gets.

Yes, leaven, baker, and now we're in my kitchen. A woman takes it and mixes it into three measures of flour, “…until all of it was leavened.” (Matthew 13:33) In the dough business, you know leaven in the right place changes the whole batch.

Salt is welcome on my counter, friend, but it's not what Jesus names. The woman mixes leaven into three measures of flour (Matthew 13:33). Leave the leaven out and my dough just lies there flat and unbothered, like a baker on a Monday morning. Close call, though.

Oil is a good thing to have around, baker, but Jesus doesn't use it in this parable. The woman takes leaven and mixes it into three measures of flour (Matthew 13:33). Leaven is what Jesus says the kingdom of heaven is like here.
Yes, all of it. Jesus says the leaven is mixed in “…until all of it was leavened.” It doesn't skip a corner of the bowl. The whole batch is changed.
Half would be a nice start, friend, but Jesus says more than that. The leaven is mixed in “…until all of it was leavened.” No part of the flour gets left out.
A top layer only would make a lopsided batch, baker. Jesus says the leaven is mixed in “…until all of it was leavened.” It's all the way through, not just the surface.

Close, but the text says the opposite. It says, “He did not tell them anything without using a parable.” (Matthew 13:34) When Jesus teaches the crowds here, everything He says comes in a parable. There aren't any plain-talk exceptions.

That's right, it's false. Matthew says, “Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables. He did not tell them anything without using a parable.” Every bit of it was a parable. Nothing was left out.
That's the one, baker. The disciples come to Jesus and say, “Explain to us the parable of the weeds in the field.” They don't ask about the other two. This is the one they want explained.

The mustard seed is a fine parable, friend, and I'd happily plant it on my counter. But it's not the one they ask about. The disciples say, “Explain to us the parable of the weeds in the field.” (Matthew 13:36) That's the one Jesus explains next.
That one's right up my alley, baker, but the disciples don't ask about it. They say, “Explain to us the parable of the weeds in the field.” So the weeds are what Jesus explains.

explanations.answer: The sons of the evil one
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, “The weeds are the sons of the evil one…” The good seed represents the sons of the kingdom, and the weeds are not the same crop. Jesus is spelling out what each piece of the parable stands for.

That's a real phrase, friend, just from another place. Jesus gave James and John, two of His disciples, the name “Sons of Thunder” (Mark 3:17). But in the weeds explanation, He says the weeds are the sons of the evil one.

Interesting guess, baker, but that phrase isn't in Jesus' explanation. He gives the weeds one name: “The weeds are the sons of the evil one…” The good seed is a different group, the sons of the kingdom.
True, baker. Jesus says, “…the enemy who sows them is the devil.” So the sneaky one who slipped away from the field gets a name. Jesus doesn't leave you guessing.
It's true, friend. When Jesus explains the parable, He says, “…the enemy who sows them is the devil.” The one who sneaked into the field has a name now.
That's right, angels. Jesus says, “…the harvesters are angels.” So when the owner in the parable tells the harvesters what to do, Jesus says angels are the ones doing it.
Makes sense, baker, since the disciples are the ones right there with Jesus. But they're the ones asking the question, not the harvesters. Jesus says, “…the harvesters are angels.”
Prophets are a reasonable guess, friend, but Jesus doesn't name them here. He says, “…the harvesters are angels.” They're the ones who do the collecting.

I wish that were what it says, friend, but it's not. Jesus says, “As the weeds are collected and burned in the fire, so will it be at the end of the age.” The weeds are not spared. I think this part is hard to hear.

That's right, it's false. Jesus says, “As the weeds are collected and burned in the fire, so will it be at the end of the age.” It's a heavy line, and I think it's fine to say so. Jesus said it plainly, so we hear it plainly.

explanations.answer: Every cause of sin and all who practice lawlessness
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Jesus says the angels will “…weed out of His kingdom every cause of sin and all who practice lawlessness.” It's one big sorting job, and it belongs to His angels. That's what He tells the disciples.

explanations.answer: Every worry and all who live in fear
explanations.explanation: That would be a nice thing to pull out of anybody's life, friend. But it isn't what Jesus says here. The angels weed out “…every cause of sin and all who practice lawlessness.”

explanations.answer: Every sickness and all who live in pain
explanations.explanation: That's a kind guess, baker, but Jesus doesn't say it in this explanation. He says the angels will weed out “…every cause of sin and all who practice lawlessness.” That's the list He gives.
True, and it's a beautiful line, baker. Jesus says, “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.” After all that weeding, this is where He lands. Nothing dim about it.
It's true, friend. Jesus says, “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.” That's how His explanation ends before He says to listen.
